food.text: Roman bread came in grades that mirrored social class. White bread was baked for the elite, darker bread for the middle class, and the darkest bread for the poor peasants. It was sometimes dipped in wine and eaten with olives, cheese and grapes.

Roman legions relied on wheat as their staple ration. They were supplied with bread and vegetables along with meats such as beef, mutton or pork. Pork was the main meat ration of the legions, while mutton was popular in Northern Gaul and Britannia.

Rome's food supply was a major political issue in the late Republic. It stayed one of the main ways the emperor expressed his relationship to the Roman people and established his role as a benefactor.

Unlike the Greek symposium, which was primarily a drinking party, the Roman convivium was focused on food. Banqueting also played a major role in Rome's communal religion. Roman traditions of conviviality were inherited in part from the Greeks and Etruscans.

At the time of Pompeii's destruction in AD 79, the city had at least 33 bakeries. Roman chefs made sweet buns flavored with blackcurrants and cheese cakes made with flour, honey, eggs, ricotta-like cheese and poppy seed.

Pompeii kept flourishing despite the political uncertainty of the Second Punic War era. Its wealth came from producing and trading wine and oil with places like Provence and Spain, along with intensive agriculture on farms around the city.

Professional bakers arrived in Rome only after the Third Macedonian War. Greek bakers came in 171 BC and became the first pistores, even though Romans had already eaten porridge and baked bread for around six hundred years.
Roman cooks favored olive oil, while butter was viewed as an undesirable Gallic foodstuff. Sweet foods such as pastries typically used honey and wine-must syrup as sweeteners.

Most Roman bread was made with sourdough. Flour and water were left in the open air to be colonised by wild yeasts, and a small amount of a successful starter was kept uncooked for the next batch. A good starter could be reused indefinitely and, as much as the flour, determined the bread's quality.

Cherries and apricots were both introduced to Rome in the 1st century BC and became popular. Peaches followed in the 1st century AD from Persia. Lemons were known but not cultivated in Italy until the Principate.
Juscellum was a broth with grated bread, eggs, sage and saffron. It is described in Apicius, a Roman recipe book of the late 4th or early 5th century.

art.text: Romans probably considered sculpture the highest form of art, though figure painting was also highly regarded. A very large body of sculpture survives from about the 1st century BC onward, but very little painting remains. Probably none of it is what a contemporary would have called top quality.

The Pantheon's coffered concrete dome, made from Roman concrete, has a central opening called the oculus. Almost two thousand years after it was built, it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

Etruscan art was produced in central Italy between the 9th and 2nd centuries BC. From around 600 BC it was heavily influenced by Greek art, which the Etruscans imported, yet it always kept distinct characteristics. It was especially strong in life-size terracotta figures on sarcophagi or temples, wall painting and bronze work.

Roman mosaic was mostly a minor art. It was used mainly for floors, curved ceilings, and walls that would get wet. Only at the very end of the period, in the late 4th century, did Christians begin using it for large religious images on the walls of their new large churches.

Nero's palace in Rome, the Domus Aurea, was built in the 60s AD, and much of it survived as grottos. Its paintings later inspired the grotesque style of painting that was popular during the Renaissance.
The Alexander Mosaic in Naples is a famous copy of a Hellenistic painting. It was originally placed in a floor in Pompeii and is much higher quality work than most Roman mosaic.

The Pantheon was begun by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa in 29–19 BC as part of a complex on the Campus Martius that also held the Baths of Agrippa and the Basilica of Neptune. The current building was completed under Hadrian and probably dedicated around AD 126. Hadrian re-inscribed it with Agrippa's original date inscription, so its construction date is uncertain.

Romans distinguished normal opus tessellatum, with tesserae mostly over 4 mm across and laid down on site, from finer opus vermiculatum. The latter was used for small panels thought to have been made in a workshop and brought to the site finished. It was a Hellenistic genre found in Italy between about 100 BC and 100 AD.
Most signed Roman mosaics carry Greek names. This suggests the artists remained mostly Greek, though probably often slaves trained up in workshops.

The only eyewitness account of the Agrippan Pantheon's decoration is in Pliny the Elder's Natural History. He wrote that its pillar capitals were made of Syracusan bronze. He also praised the Caryatides by Diogenes of Athens, which formed the columns, as masterpieces.

In the late 4th century BC, Pompeii began expanding beyond its old nucleus. The street plan of the new areas was more regular and conformed to Hippodamus's street plan. In the early 3rd century BC the city walls were reinforced in Sarno stone.

The Pantheon's pediment was decorated with relief sculpture, probably of gilded bronze. Holes for the clamps that held it suggest the design was an eagle within a wreath, with ribbons extending into the corners of the pediment.

war.text: Unlike the later Pax Romana of the Roman Empire, republican Rome was in a state of near-perpetual war. Its first enemies were its Latin and Etruscan neighbours and the Gauls, who sacked Rome around 387 BC. Rome went on to conquer most of the Italian peninsula in a century and then waged three wars against Carthage. Over the Republic's lifetime its control grew from the city's immediate surroundings to hegemony over the entire Mediterranean world, through a long series of difficult conquests.

When Rome went to war with Carthage in 264 BC, it had the stronger army but Carthage ruled the sea. The Romans, novice shipwrights, used a shipwrecked Carthaginian quinquereme as a blueprint. Their copies were heavier, and so slower and less maneuverable.

Around 387 BC, a Gallic tribe called the Senones, led by Brennus, invaded Northern Italy and routed the Romans at the Battle of the Allia, about 11 Roman miles north of Rome. In the panicked flight the Gauls killed soldiers blocking one another's paths, and men weighed down by their armour drowned in the Tiber. Rome was then sacked by the Senones; according to Livy, once the elderly patricians sitting in their porticoes were attacked, no living being was spared and the houses were looted and set on fire, while Plutarch says the Gauls killed everyone they captured, including women, children and the elderly. Modern scholars doubt the extent of the destruction, since there is no archaeological trace of damage from the sack.

Roman armies occupied Spain in the early 2nd century BC but met stiff resistance. The Celtiberian stronghold of Numantia became the centre of Spanish resistance to Rome in the 140s and 130s BC, and it fell and was razed to the ground in 133 BC. In 105 BC the Celtiberians drove the Cimbri and Teutones out of northern Spain, though these tribes had crushed Roman arms in southern Gaul and inflicted 80,000 casualties on the Roman army. The conquest of Hispania was completed in 19 BC, but at a heavy cost.

The Roman fleet that grew from copied Carthaginian designs fought in the 256 BC battle of Ecnomus, possibly the largest naval battle in history by the number of combatants. In 241 BC the Romans destroyed the Carthaginian fleet at the Battle of the Aegates Islands, ending the war.

The Social War was fought largely from 91 to 88 BC between Rome and several of its autonomous Italian allies, and began when the people of Asculum, fearing Roman discovery of their hostage exchange, killed the Roman praetor Quintus Servilius and his legate Fonteius, then killed all the Romans in the city and ransacked their goods. Rome cut the rebels into northern and southern sectors, and Lucius Cornelius Sulla defeated those in the south. Offers of Roman citizenship to towns that had not revolted or would lay down arms drained support from the rebels, and the Romans moved quickly and brutally to suppress the attempt to incite rebellion in Etruria and Umbria.

In the Latin War of 340 to 338 BC, Rome defeated a coalition of Latins at the battles of Vesuvius and the Trifanum, and the Latins submitted to Roman rule. The war broke out after Rome had won two battles against the Samnites between 343 and 341 BC but could not consolidate its gains, because former Latin allies went to war with it. The article gives no casualty figures for these battles.

The Battle of Actium in 31 BC between Augustus and Mark Antony marked the peak of the Roman fleet arm. After Augustus' victory, most of the Roman fleet was dismantled and burned. From the 160s until the 4th century AD, no major fleet actions were recorded, and many galley crews were disbanded or put to work for entertainment, in mock battles or in handling the sail-like sun-screens in the larger Roman arenas.

The Romans effectively completed the conquest of their immediate Etruscan neighbors after Veii fell in 396 BC. Earlier, they had been defeated by the Veientani at the battle of the Cremera in 477 BC. Resistance in Etruria was finally crushed in 265 to 264 BC.

Merchant ships such as the naves onerariae were pressed into military service, for instance to carry troops to North Africa in the Second Punic War. In 204 BCE, Scipio Africanus ordered the impressment of merchantmen for the invasion of Africa, four hundred ships according to Livy.

During the Second Punic War, Pompeii remained faithful to Rome unlike many southern cities, while Hannibal's invasion threatened many cities. As a result, an additional internal wall was built of tufa and the outer façade raised. This produced a double parapet with a wider wall-walk.

Rome's sixth king, Servius Tullius, is said by Livy to have gone to war with Veii and the rest of the Etruscans. According to the Fasti Triumphales, he celebrated three triumphs over the Etruscans, including on 25 November 571 BC and 25 May 567 BC.

literature.text: Formal Latin literature began in 240 BC, when the first stage play in Latin was performed in Rome. This was one year after the First Punic War ended. Latin literature then flourished for the next six centuries.

Virgil's Aeneid describes how the Trojan hero Aeneas became the ancestor of the Roman people. It gave divine justification for Roman rule over the world. Although Virgil died before he could finish it, the poem was soon regarded as the greatest work of Latin literature.

Ovid's works were wildly popular, yet Augustus exiled the poet, in what the article calls one of literary history's great mysteries. Ovid's own oblique explanation was carmen et error, meaning "a poem and a mistake".

Livy's History of Rome was written in Latin between 27 and 9 BC and originally had 142 books. Only 35 survive, about a quarter of the work. It begins with the legends of Aeneas and Troy and runs down to Livy's own time under Augustus.

Livius Andronicus was a Greek prisoner of war brought to Rome as a slave in 272 BC. He adapted Greek dramas for the Roman stage and translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin using the traditional Saturnian meter.

Gnaeus Naevius, a Roman citizen, continued the tradition of reworking Greek dramas. He also created a new type, the fabula praetexta, tragedies based on Roman myths and history, starting in 222 BC. Later he wrote an epic poem in Saturnian meter about the First Punic War, in which he had fought.

Christian Latin literature took shape in the 4th and 5th centuries through church fathers such as Augustine of Hippo, Jerome and Ambrose, and the first great Christian poet, Prudentius. Some writing by Christian women also survives, including the prison diary of the martyr Perpetua of Carthage and the pilgrim Egeria's account of a pilgrimage.

Livius Andronicus was a Greek captive from Tarentum, a city Rome captured in 272 BC. He was sold as a slave in the 3rd century BC and put to work as a tutor for his master's children. After he obtained his freedom, Livius Andronicus continued to live in Rome and became the first schoolmaster to follow Greek methods of education.

Livy admitted that the early years of Rome were profoundly ahistorical. He wrote that traditions about the time before the city's foundation were better suited to adorn the creations of a poet than the authentic records of a historian. His first book is a major source for the legend of Romulus and Remus.

Livius Andronicus was a Greek captive from Tarentum sold as a slave in the 3rd century BC and employed as a tutor. After gaining his freedom he became the first schoolmaster in Rome to follow Greek methods and translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin verse.

In Book IX of Ovid's Metamorphoses, dated to 8 CE, Iphis's father declares, while his wife is pregnant, that he will kill the child if it is a girl. She bears a girl and hides her sex by giving her a name of ambiguous gender, Iphis. When the "son" is thirteen, the father chooses a golden-haired maiden, Ianthe, as the "boy's" bride. The love of the two girls is written sympathetically, but as the wedding nears Iphis recoils, calling her love "monstrous and unheard of", and the gods hear her moans and turn her into a man.

In the Aeneid, Virgil draws on the Greek tradition of pederasty in a military setting by portraying the love between Nisus and Euryalus, whose military valor marks them as solidly Roman men. He describes their love as pius, linking it to pietas, the supreme virtue of the hero Aeneas himself. According to a biography by Suetonius, Virgil had a marked sexual preference for boys.

science.text: The Roman Empire was one of the most technologically advanced civilizations of antiquity. Some of its concepts and inventions were forgotten in Late Antiquity and the early Middle Ages. In areas such as civil engineering and construction materials, and in inventions such as the mechanical reaper, the Romans were not improved upon until the 19th century.

The Romans reached high levels of technology in large part because they borrowed from other peoples. Their sources included the Greeks, Etruscans and Celts. Roman engineering was often a blend of borrowed ideas rather than purely local invention.

Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried under 4 to 6 m of volcanic ash and pumice in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Pyroclastic flows of scorching ash incinerated or suffocated the people who had not fled, and a 2010 study found that heat, not suffocation, was the main cause of death: exposure to at least 250 °C was enough to kill instantly, even for people sheltered inside buildings. The bodies decayed in the ash, leaving voids that allowed archaeologists to create moulds of figures in their final moments of life.

Roman technical skill lived inside trades such as stonemasonry, passed from master to apprentice. Because few sources survive, it is theorized that tradesmen kept their knowledge secret. Vitruvius, Pliny the Elder and Frontinus are among the few writers who published technical information about Roman technology.

Rome and its surrounding area contained various types of volcanic materials, and the Romans experimented with them to create building materials. The durability of Roman roads, dams and buildings is accounted for by the building techniques and practices used in their construction. Many of these structures survive to this day.

The Romans built dams to store water for irrigation. They understood that spillways were necessary to prevent the erosion of earth-packed banks. This shows practical knowledge of how moving water wears away soil.
Roman bridges were built with stone or concrete and used the arch. The Pons Aemilius, built in 142 BC and later named Ponte Rotto, meaning broken bridge, is the oldest Roman stone bridge in Rome.

Romans had a corpus of manuals on basic mathematics and science, including many books by Archimedes, Ctesibius, Heron and Euclid. Not all of the manuals available to the Romans have survived, as lost works illustrate.

politics.text: According to tradition, Rome became a republic in 509 BC, when kings were replaced with rule by elected magistrates. Over the following centuries it grew from a regional power in Latium into the dominant force in Italy and beyond.

In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus and made him princeps, or foremost, with proconsular imperium. This began the Principate, the first epoch of Roman imperial history. Although the republic stood in name, Augustus had all meaningful authority.

Rome's rule spread across the Mediterranean and beyond. At its height the empire covered around 5 million square kilometres in AD 117, with an estimated 50 to 90 million inhabitants, roughly 20% of the world's population at the time.

The Western Roman Empire formally fell in 476 AD, when Romulus Augustus was deposed and Italy fell under the control of Odoacer. Italy had been invaded several times by wandering Germanic peoples, and Rome itself was sacked in 410 by Alaric's Visigoths and in 455 by the Vandals under Genseric. Italy was afterwards ruled by the Ostrogoths, then briefly reconquered by the Byzantine Empire after Justinian's invasion in 535 brought twenty years of disastrous war.

Rome's victory over Carthage in the First Punic War brought its first two provinces outside the Italian peninsula, Sicily and Sardinia. Parts of Spain, then called Hispania, followed. Rome thus became the capital of an overseas empire for the first time.

Julius Caesar was briefly perpetual dictator in 44 BC before he was assassinated by a faction that opposed his concentration of power. The faction was driven from Rome and defeated at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC by Mark Antony and Caesar's adopted son Octavian.

In 87 BC Marius and Cinna took Rome and killed the consul Gnaeus Octavius, then avenged their partisans by conducting a massacre. After Sulla's first march on Rome in 88 BC, where his legions killed all who showed support for Marius, he returned in 83 BC for a second march and began a time of terror: thousands of nobles, knights and senators were executed. Sulla held two dictatorships and one more consulship, which began the crisis and decline of the Roman Republic.

In 286 AD Diocletian moved the imperial residence for the western territories from Rome to Mediolanum. In 293 AD he subdivided Italy into provinces and ended its special juridical privileges. Italy thereby lost its precedence over the provinces.

After Augustus died, Tiberius was not an enthusiast for political affairs. After agreement with the Senate, he retired to Capri in 26 AD. He left control of Rome to the praetorian prefect Sejanus until 31 AD, and then to Macro from 31 to 37 AD.

In 195 BCE the consul Cato the Censor argued to keep the Lex Oppia, which limited women's display of gold and clothing. He held that personal morality and self-restraint were self-evidently inadequate controls on indulgence and luxury, and that Roman women had shown their appetites, once corrupted, knew no limits and must be restrained. According to Livy, he called the protesting matrons an "army of women" and described their craving for spending as a particularly female disease that could never be cured, only suppressed. The matrons protested in large numbers and the laws were abolished in 193 BCE.

The Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, suspicious of plots by the Byzantines, turned on the Roman senatorial class and began persecuting it. He went so far as to have the philosopher Boethius executed, even though Boethius was attempting to end the persecution. Theodoric died in 526, which ended the persecution.

philosophy.text: Philosophy was brought to Italy by Pythagoras, who founded a school of philosophy in Crotone, in Magna Graecia. Later Magna Graecia produced major thinkers including Parmenides, Zeno, Empedocles and Gorgias.
Interest in philosophy was first excited at Rome in 155 BC by an Athenian embassy. It consisted of the Academic skeptic Carneades, the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon and the Peripatetic Critolaus.

Roman philosophy was heavily influenced by the ancient Greeks and the schools of Hellenistic philosophy. Even so, unique developments in philosophical schools of thought occurred during the Roman period.

In the Roman view, religion was practical and tied to the mos maiorum, "the way of the ancestors", which was central to Roman identity. The Romans credited their success as a world power to their collective piety in keeping good relations with the gods.
Empedocles is best known for originating the cosmogonic theory of the four classical elements. He is considered the last Greek philosopher to write in verse.

Pythagoras is considered "the Father of Ethical Vegetarianism". He believed that the highest level of spiritual and physical health required a vegetarian diet that excluded meats and other flesh foods.

Romans regarded philosophical education as distinctly Greek. Students who wanted to study it usually had to travel abroad to Greece, so Romans focused their efforts instead on building schools of law and rhetoric.

Scholars debate whether the surviving fragments of Empedocles' teaching belong to two separate poems, "Purifications" and "On Nature", or to a single poem with two titles. Some argue that "Purifications" names only the first part of a larger work called "On Nature".
The Roman government expelled many rhetoricians and philosophers in 161 BC. Their tutors had such great influence on the opinions and actions of their students that the state acted against them.

culture.text: Life in ancient Rome revolved around monumental architecture like the Colosseum and the Pantheon, but most people lived in packed apartment blocks called insulae. The city of Rome was the largest megalopolis of its time, with a population that may well have exceeded one million people.

Roman religion was part of daily life. Each home had a household shrine where prayers and libations were offered to the family's domestic deities, and neighbourhood shrines, springs and groves dotted the city. The Roman calendar itself was structured around religious observances.
The Colosseum, built around 70 to 80 AD, was the largest amphitheatre ever built in the Roman Empire. It could originally seat 60,000 spectators and was used for gladiatorial combat.

The Vestals were the one major public role reserved solely for Roman women. They were forbidden marriage or sex for thirty years, and devoted themselves to rituals deemed necessary for Rome's survival that the male priestly colleges could not perform. A Vestal found to have broken her vow of chastity was held to have polluted her office, and the penalty was to be given food and water and entombed alive.

After the Roman defeat at Cannae, the Lex Oppia of 215 BCE restricted women's gold and silver, expensive clothing, and use of chariots and litters. When it was reviewed in 195 BCE, Cato the Censor argued to keep it, but large numbers of Roman matrons protested publicly. The law was abolished in 193 BCE.

Roman priesthoods were held by the elite, with no separation of church and state. Julius Caesar became pontifex maximus before he was elected consul. Priests married, raised families and led politically active lives.

Emperor Hadrian founded the Athenaeum, a school for literary and scientific studies named after Athens. Poets, orators and critics recited their compositions there, sometimes in the presence of emperors. Its site was discovered in 2009 during Metro C excavations in Piazza Venezia.

The Vestals tended Rome's sacred hearth for centuries as a state-supported priesthood of six women. They were bound by a vow of chastity that was strictly enforced: a Vestal polluted by the loss of her chastity while in office was buried alive. The order was disbanded only under Christian domination, after Theodosius I extinguished Vesta's sacred fire and vacated her temple.
In 42 BCE Roman women, led by Hortensia, successfully protested against laws designed to tax them. They used the argument of no taxation without representation.
The Roman triumph was at its core a religious procession. The victorious general displayed his piety by dedicating a portion of his spoils to the gods, especially Jupiter, who embodied just rule.

Astrologers and magicians were officially expelled from Rome at various times, notably in 139 BC and 33 BC. In 16 BC Tiberius expelled them under extreme penalty because an astrologer had predicted his death. In the late 1st century AD, Tacitus observed that astrologers "would always be banned and always retained at Rome".

The dies Alliensis, the 'Day of the Allia', was regarded as an ill-omened day in the Roman calendar, and public and ritual activity was avoided on it. Yet the tradition is only attested from the 1st century BC, so it likely reflects later reconstruction rather than continuous observance.

In 204 BCE the Roman Senate permitted the worship of Cybele, or the Great Mother. Her religion came from Phrygia to Greece and then to Egypt and Italy. She was a healing and protecting goddess, and a guardian of fertility and wild nature.

Under Theodosius II, the Athenaeum's staff included three orators, ten grammarians, five sophists, one philosopher and two lawyers. The institution seems to have kept a high reputation until the sixth century.

After the Roman fleet was largely disbanded, many galley crews were employed for entertainment in mock battles or in handling the sail-like sun-screens in the larger Roman arenas. Galley crewmen even called themselves milites, 'soldiers', rather than nautae, 'sailors'.
